# The Value of Disagreement: Why Good Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## The Consensus Trap

There is a widely held belief, embedded in how most organizations operate, that a successful meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. The goal, we assume, is alignment. If the room ends in agreement, the meeting worked; if people leave still arguing, it failed. This assumption shapes everything from how we run discussions to how we evaluate leaders. A manager who "builds consensus" is praised. A meeting that ends with unresolved tension is seen as unproductive, even embarrassing.

But this way of thinking contains a serious flaw: agreement is not the same thing as understanding. In fact, agreement can be a mask. When a group converges quickly on a decision, it is often unclear whether everyone has genuinely reached the same conclusion for the same reasons, or whether some people have simply stopped voicing doubts. Silence gets recorded as consent. Reluctance gets recorded as support. And the meeting ends with a warm feeling of unity that may not survive contact with reality.
